segments.t: At the start of this episode, Chef Barinov feeds his fish Arkady before welcoming Alexey Smolin, a Michelin inspector visiting the restaurant. Even after an awkward spill, the inspector praises the chef's signature tasting menu.
Now let's go back through their conversation line by line and unpack the Russian phrasing.
'Do not look at me like that.' Barinov shows an honest mood with the inspector, using "smotri" (from "smotret", "look") alongside "ne" ("not") to shape the meaning.
'You must not be overfed right now.' Barinov offers an honest line right away, leaning on "nelzya" ("not allowed") before closing the thought with "seychas" ("now").
'Hello, Viktor Petrovich.' The inspector brings a steady view in the room, weaving "zdravstvuyte" ("hello") together with "viktor" ("Viktor") just the way native speakers do.
'I am inspecting your restaurant.' The inspector conveys a pointed approach right away, joining "inspektiruyu" ("I inspect") to "restoran" ("restaurant") so every word pulls its weight.
'Is everything alright with you?' Barinov probes frankly in the scene, anchoring the Russian line on "poryadke" ("order") and "vami" ("you") without extra filler.
'Yes, it is just so unexpected.' The inspector adopts a playful tempo across the room, anchoring the Russian line on "prosto" ("just") and "neozhidanno" ("unexpected") without extra filler.
'Hello, I am very pleased to meet you.' Barinov maintains a lively style as they talk, putting "zdravstvuyte" ("hello") alongside "ochen" ("very much") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.

'Your signature set is simply excellent.' The inspector strikes an easygoing rhythm as they talk, linking "avtorskiy" ("author's, creator's") directly with "set" ("tasting set"), since Russian drops "is" and "are" in the present.

'It overshadowed that unpleasant incident.' The inspector displays a steady tempo at once, putting "zakryl" ("passed, closed") alongside "nepriyatnyy" ("unpleasant") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
'Thank you for the kind words.' Barinov takes a playful mood in the room, putting "spasibo" ("thank you") alongside "dobryye" ("good, kind") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
'Just do not worry.' Barinov sets a serious note across the room, putting "tolko" ("only") alongside "volnuytes" ("worry") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
'We will wash everything out quickly.' Barinov conveys a grounded tone toward the inspector, linking "bystro" ("quickly"), "otstirayem" ("we will wash out"), and "my" ("we") in one brisk exchange.
The Michelin inspector seems genuinely impressed by the tasting menu, though trouble is just around the corner in the kitchen. Until next time!
